item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Friday, 25 September 2026
item.description:
Tipa gets Valheim’s Elder kill and achievement, then builds a dojo to grind mace and blocking skills before braving a fresh swamp.

Sey’s roundup spotlights TOEM 2, Songs of Glimmerwick, Okko The Exiled, and Christopher Larkin’s Moonlighter 2 soundtrack with plenty of wishlist energy.

Bhagpuss sizes up Neverness To Everness’s next update and wonders if its breakneck, wildly varied content drops have left the game with an identity problem.

Kimimi makes the case that Deadalus, aka Robotica, works better as a roguelite than an FPS, with randomized floors and run-managing tension.

Mailvaltar restarts Dune: Awakening again, sold on singleplayer’s permanent Deep Desert bases, no housing sprawl, and less multiplayer lag.

Joar is happily catching up in Guild Wars 2, finding it more compelling than WoW lately while still only considering a Dawntrail return in FFXIV.

Emily vents about the gamer instinct to brute-force mountains in Skyrim, The Witcher 3, and Death Stranding instead of finding the obvious easier path.

Wilhelm hits Stardew Valley year three after finally cracking Skull Cavern, cashing Qi’s reward, and turning farm automation into more Calico Desert time.

Aneesh shares a quick linkpost pointing to Substack’s ‘cool new way to post’ and his own blyg site.

Tim Bray argues POSIWID is a lousy shortcut, saying systems have multiple purposes and we need sharper language for talking about GenAI, capitalism, and power.

Dave Winer shares a new Frontier example script for building an RSS feed from a single Mastodon account, a small peek at the project’s progress.

Andrew Plotkin reflects on John M. Ford twenty years on, revisiting Aspects and the comfort, questions, and rereads his work still inspires.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Thursday, 24 September 2026
item.description:
Shintar marks 1,500 SWTOR posts with a stats-and-search-terms look back, including why “swtor private server” keeps sending people over.

Krista is back in Skyrim on PS5 with a Dark Elf, hoping this cozy autumn replay finally becomes the run where she finishes it.

Marc revisits James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing as a fascinating early-2000s Bond game and an overlooked precursor to 007 First Light.

Sweetie rounds up dream remakes, especially Persona 1 and 2 and Dragon Quest IV, with an eye toward accessibility and preserving their charm.

Wilhelm argues EVE Online’s Cradle of War update fixates on Ansiblex nerfs, making nullsec fights duller even as alliances quickly adapt.

The Chronicler spotlights Revolutions: France 1820-1880, a negotiation-heavy political simulation where alliances, coups, and presentation do the heavy lifting.

Anarchae writes candidly about friendship anxiety, ADHD, and the guilt of drifting from people as a job ending stirs up autumn melancholy.

Joar says good live music is more than familiar songs: crowd energy, the room, and bands like the Cheektones make the night work.

Brennan offers a beginner-friendly static site generator primer, while sensibly insisting you learn plain HTML and CSS before adding abstraction.

Cristian highlights WhatsApp terms that grant broad rights over uploaded content, and notes the same Meta-wide logic reaches Instagram, Messenger, and more.

JJM traces a long path from WordStar and joe through vim and neovim to emacs, finally making it click by bringing vim habits along.

Kelly does the unnerving math on how many blog posts and words he may have left, then turns it into a gentle reminder about limited time.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Wednesday, 23 September 2026
item.description:
Stargrace’s WoW week brought 2.3 million gold, forgotten pet sales, alt leveling via pet battles, and a low-pressure plan for WoW Forever.

Syp enjoys Fallout 76’s permission to be gloriously weird, then pivots to Diablo III as the perfect loud, clicky comfort-food ARPG.

UltrViolet wraps Final Fantasy XIV: Endwalker 6.0 with big praise for its finale, voice acting, and nihilist streak, plus some truly hated quest design.

Margot found Firewatch a compact storytelling knockout, with strong voice acting and Steam Deck-friendly play, though the first-person movement may trigger motion sickness.

Shintar rounds up WoW Forever memes and fan reactions, capturing the giddy, slightly unhinged hype train before launch.

Zack says Life is Strange: True Colors is the series’ best yet, praising Deck Nine’s writing and all-at-once episodic structure.

Wilhelm’s WoW Forever beta take is refreshingly lukewarm: huge queues were beta doing beta things, and the vanilla-plus vibe seems perfectly fine.

Roger recommends Nicol Williamson’s atmospheric Hobbit audio adaptation, with standout character voices despite a few abridgement gaps and minor pronunciation quirks.

Warner’s latest reading roundup leans dark, hopping from AI safety and media failure to improv, play, and one welcome farm kitten.

Axxuy resurfaces after a maddening TCP issue that broke most internet use, with a timely reminder to actually test your backups too.

Juhis makes a practical case for print-friendly websites, with CSS media-query basics and a reader-first argument for offering more ways to use a page.

Scopique digs into CSS and even plain HTML basics, reflecting on how chasing the cool stuff too early can leave gaps.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Tuesday, 22 September 2026
item.description:
Tipa digs into Guild Wars 2’s Visions of Eternity, where Asura chaos, Vloxx’s reality reboot, and the Commander role all rub her the wrong way.

Bhagpuss wrestles with gaming overload versus drought, using Xbox cloud limits and GeForce Now to poke at the hobby’s endless contradictions.

Oya has a blast with Astro Bot’s giant sponge power-up, gleefully smashing through a hot-bath maze with haptics making the chaos even sweeter.

Wilhelm starts No Man’s Sky Expedition 23, flips multiplayer off, and enjoys Cosmos as a nostalgia-heavy tour through the game’s past updates.

Tobold says Avalon: The Riven Veil looks great, but long setup, dense iconography, and a three-hour-plus runtime make it a rough fit for game night.

Anarchae’s weekly links bounce from bioblitzes and solo TTRPGs to Ace Combat, disability discourse, nostalgic music, and fish-versus-nuclear-plant climate weirdness.

Jamie Zawinski previews DNA Lounge’s Folsom weekend lineup, from Brüt and Bare Chest to Brooke Candy and Violet Chachki.

Joel’s weeknotes mix Mexican Independence Day, War of the Worlds, Final Fantasy IV, Gunstar Heroes, and a pleasantly busy blogging week.

Emily finds Hyacinth a refreshing Bridgerton lead, with Italian diary translation, jewel hunting, and thankfully less forced-marriage melodrama.

Jeff argues Raspberry Pi 5’s firmware RAM lock makes technical sense but still undercuts the Pi’s hardware-hacking ethos.

Bruce Schneier spotlights GPT-6 Astra cracking an old Enigma message by building its own simulator and Bombe around a ROSENOW crib.

Dave Winer has Claude catalog Atlantis verbs, wants Frontier to get websockets, and keeps chipping away at old Mac-era breakage.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Monday, 21 September 2026
item.description:
Stargrace starts a Cartograph solo RPG notebook adventure, mapping scholars and sentient wasps with fountain-pen-loving enthusiasm.

CrazyKinux boils EVE fix ideas down to a livelier New Eden, with shifting resources and space weather driving players into motion.

Kimimi loves Ace Combat X for its weighty mission choices, but it’s the radio chatter that really sells the drama.

Shintar peeks into WoW Classic Forever’s beta, noting huge queues, bustling starter zones, and the new tauren Plainsrunning racial.

Wilhelm checks Fantasy Critic League week 38, where Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter and Fire Emblem land big review scores.

The Chronicler finds La Der des Ders packs the whole First World War into a brisk evening wargame without skimping on strategic texture.

Aneesh revisits Trinity’s motorcycle scene in Matrix Reloaded and comes away impressed—and missing his bike.

Ramen Junkie rounds up GameStop retro carts, CHVRCHES album teases, and the ongoing annoyance of AI bot spam.

Tan’s weekly digest covers a rough parenting week, an encouraging first Scouts session, banking frustrations, and teaching kids on a cute keyboard.

Kelly weighs Anthropic and OpenAI backing AI regulation, arguing safety rules matter most where systems can harm vulnerable people or control machines.

Brennan argues LLMs make scraping, spam, and bad-faith extraction cheap and easy, turning the open web into a much harsher place.

Cristian sketches his ideal Linux distro: Mint-like stability, Fedora-fresh apps, GNOME, easy installs, solid gaming, and definitely no AUR.
